newsitem.title: THAILAND: Moody's downgrades seen stalling Thai rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Moody's downgrades seen stalling Thai rate cuts.

text.p: Moody's downgrade of Thailand's sovereign and bank deposit ratings on Wednesday could stall a planned interest rate cut, possibly dealing another blow to the country's struggling economy, analysts said.

The downgrade came as no surprise to a market already reeling from a finance sector crisis brought on by a slumping property market, but most analysts agreed the move would force more local borrowers into the domestic market to raise funds.

The larger number of borrowers tapping the domestic market, aiming to avoid the prospect of higher offshore funding costs, could force a tightening in liquidity which many fear will take a rate cut off the cards for this year.
"Banks and finance firms will need to mobilise more deposits, making it harder for rates to come down," said Kavee Chukijkasem, analyst at Capital Nomura Securities Plc.

Moody's Investors Service said it had downgraded Thailand's foreign currency ceilings for bonds to A3 from A2, a move foreshadowed by a warning in February that the U.S.-based agency had placed the ratings under review.
Moody's also trimmed the senior debt and deposit ratings of five Thai banks to A3 from A2.

"The exact impact of the downgrades will be determined by economic indicators coming out in the next several months. I don't expect the level of non-performing loans carried by financial institutions to ease this year," said Kavee.
Moody's said the cuts reflected concerns over asset quality and instability of the Thai financial system.
Analysts were divided on when the current economic slowdown and financial sector problems would begin to ease.
Kavee said most creditor banks were keeping their fingers crossed that sour property loans would peak this year and government rescue measures would start producing results.
"Everyone should accept the reality...I don't think we will see a quick recovery this year," he added.

"Moody's has been reasonably objective," a foreign analyst said. "(The downgrades) have potential medium-term negative reaction. They should make it slightly more expensive for Thai institutions to borrow."

Most analysts said Moody's announcements had already been discounted in local markets. The composite SET Index dipped about seven points in mid-morning trade but recovered to stay just inside positive territory at the lunch break.
The baht was also steady and quoted at 26.101/106 against the dollar at 0757 GMT after hitting a low of 26.117 earlier.
Analysts said Thai corporate offshore borrowing had risen by about 30-40 basis points since last September when Moody's downgraded the country's short-term debt ratings.
Supawat Saichua, of Krungthai Thanakit Plc, said the foreign funding costs of Thai borrowers would at most rise another 10 basis points because of the most recent downgrades.
"Although an improvement of Thai fundamentals would take time, we should see some better figures late this year especially from a narrowing current account deficit and reduced imports," he said.
Kavee said it was premature to say if the Moody's downgrades would prompt ratings agency Standard & Poor's to follow suit.
"S&P reviews country ratings quarterly," he said. "It looks at Thailand from a different angle than that of Moody's. Much will depend on how the property loan figures look like later this year."

S&P said on March 18 it had affirmed Thailand's single-A long term and A-1 short term foreign currency debt ratings. It said the country's financial outlook remained stable but noted heightened risk in the banking sector.
